title: Coffee with Priya
description: Demo conversation (synthetic, for the demo account). Alex and Priya go from free will and determinism to Stoicism, detour into a podcast they both follow, then return to Stoicism as a way to handle Alex's job stress.

utterances.text: Okay, I ordered the oat latte again. Every single time.
See, that's my whole point from the other night. Did you actually choose the oat latte, or was it chosen for you like ten years ago?
Oh no. We're doing this before I've had any caffeine?
We're doing this. If every thought comes from your brain, and your brain comes from genes and everything that ever happened to you, where's the free part?
I mean, it feels free. Right now I feel like I could get up and order a matcha.
Sure, but feeling free isn't the same as being free. A thermostat would probably feel free too if it could feel things.
Okay, that's rude to me and to the thermostat.
Honestly, I think I'm a compatibilist? Maybe it's all caused, but if I'm acting on my own reasons, that's the only kind of free that matters.
That always sounds like a cop-out to me. It's redefining the word so you don't have to feel bad.
Maybe. But what's the alternative, that nobody's responsible for anything? That's worse.
Not that. Just way less smug about people who mess up. And about ourselves when we do well.
Hm. Yeah, okay, I'll give you the smug part.
Which is kind of why I got into the Stoics, actually. They were total determinists, and they still cared a ton about how you act.
Wait, really? I thought Stoicism was just, like, don't have feelings.
No, that's the internet version. The core thing is splitting the world into what's up to you and what isn't. Your judgments, your effort. That's yours. Other people, your reputation, not yours.
Okay, that I actually like.
Marcus Aurelius was running an empire during a plague, writing in his journal that you can only control how you respond.
Which is wild because if anyone could control people it was the emperor.
Right! Oh, that reminds me, did you hear Small Hours last week? The guy who walked across Mongolia?
Yes! The camel episode! I listened to it on the bus and laughed out loud like a weirdo.
When the camel just sits down in the middle of the river and refuses to move?
And he waits for, what, four hours?
Five! And he says he read Seneca to the camel.
That's why you brought it up. Okay, that tracks.
It's the most Stoic thing I've ever heard. He couldn't control the camel, so he just sat there.
Okay, anyway, sorry, back to the actual point.
No, but it connects. Because, honestly, I need some of the camel guy's energy right now.
Is this the work thing?
Yeah. The claims team rewrote the requirements on Monday, my manager asked why the screens weren't done on Wednesday, and I keep waking up at four replaying meetings.
Okay, so let's actually do the Stoic split on that. What's up to you in that mess?
Um. How fast I work. Whether I flag stuff early. Whether I keep redoing screens at eleven at night.
And what's not up to you?
The claims team. My manager's mood. Whether leadership changes the roadmap again.
So how much of the four a.m. replaying is about the first list?
Wow. Okay. Basically none of it.
That's the thing. Epictetus has this line that it's not things that upset us, it's our judgments about things.
But that feels like telling me to just accept a bad job.
No. Leaving is also up to you. You can accept what you can't change and still walk away.
Yeah. And there's the other thing, the studio offer. I haven't told you much about it yet.
The exhibit design place? I thought you were just humoring them.
I was, and now they want a final round. Part of me wants to say yes just to stop feeling like this.
Then do it for a better reason than escaping. What do you want true about your work in a year?
That I'm proud of it. That I'm not dreading Sunday nights.
That's a good list. And notice, it's about you, not about your manager.
Okay. Writing that down. Also, I still think I chose the oat latte.
Ha, fine. We'll fight about free will next week.
